cells.tense: Here and now the pen is in hand, and the good you feel around what is growing is yours to say out loud.
cells.ask: When something good happens this week, name who made it good, to their face, before the week is out.
cells.core:
You know how to care for a thing that hasn't finished growing. You don't rush it and you don't walk away — the reminder texts, the remembering of what matters to someone, the showing up before it's interesting. That patient attention is running clean, and the people around you can feel it.
The pen is in your hand on the saying-so. When something good is happening with the people you tend, you decide whether it gets called good while it's happening or just felt quietly. Both are running on the same current this week. Name what's happening, to the people it involves, before the moment closes. That is the same act of care as the feeding, only louder.
cells.sheetLine: You tend what's growing and you tell the truth about it.
cells.verb: Turning shared feeling into something that feeds the people it happens to
cells.place: In the care of what hasn't finished growing yet

cells.tense: Ahead is a version where the thing is finished and thriving, and you are already sprinting toward it.
cells.ask: Pick the one thing you've pushed hardest this week. Do less on it, with someone watching, and let them take the next step alone.
cells.core:
You're managing the growth ahead of the growth. The check-ins, the gear for a hobby that's three weeks old, the plans for what this becomes — all of it pushed harder than it's ready for. You're living in the finished version, so today keeps getting demoted to a rehearsal for something better.
The push is eating the thing the push was for. The growing things don't need the full plan made for them. They need you in the room, not ahead of it. A place that only runs in present tense doesn't hold the future well. Let the current version be the version. The result is the practicing kind, not the promising kind.

cells.tense: The door you keep standing at is already behind you, and the care has gone thin from the doorway.
cells.ask: Pick the one person or thing you're still tending. Read about the thing itself for ten minutes, without checking on anyone, without producing anything.
cells.core:
You tend what's growing and you don't arrive at it. The feeding happens and the enjoyment doesn't — you keep the thing alive but you don't sit down inside it, don't let it be a pleasure. The door is behind you now, and the instructions you're following come from past it. Showing up became a job done competently from the threshold.
Depth on the subject itself is the missing piece — the mind going far enough into the thing to actually see it instead of just service it. That's not pushing more care in. It's charging the deeper side of the same line. Go in past the maintenance and find out what the thing actually is to you.
cells.sheetLine: You tend it, but you stopped going in.

cells.tense: You are already the one shaping what matters to the people around you, and you describe it as if it were just happening.
cells.ask: Say out loud once, to the person or into the air: this is mine. Choose the thing you keep calling the group's or the family's.
cells.core:
You're already the one deciding what matters to the people around you — what gets remembered, what gets called a big deal, what gets celebrated and when. That's what caring for what's growing does. But it gets described as if it were just happening, or as if the group did it, or as if it were only logistics. The good taste in what's being built is yours, and it stays unclaimed.
The unclaimed version is also the scattered version. The instinct is running across twenty small decisions, not gathered into something you could steer by. Gathering it isn't a new skill. It's claiming what's already going on. Start by naming one thing that's really yours, not everybody's.
cells.sheetLine: You're already shaping what matters, and you haven't claimed it.

attempts.check: Two claims the record does not support and I cut: that the balanced card is 'free to feed next' (mechanism language, not a fact about the person), and that the past-anchor in Too Much or Too Little is a located room in their life — it may name the anchor, never the room's contents. A reader could reasonably say 'the joy isn't mine, it's the group's,' which is fine: the cell only claims authorship of the tending, not of the feeling. The ask survives being wrong at every status — each one is a doable act that teaches something about where the tending starts and stops, whether or not the read lands. The sentence that serves me more than them: any line that congratulates the reader for a method I invented — cut before it reached the cells.
